- **self**: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even (14/5)

## How it works

- [statement] On-demand bills consumed request units; provisioned bills allocated capacity per hour even when idle. Stable utilization favors provisioned economics, while intermittent demand avoids idle throughput charges with on-demand. (high confidence) — https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CostOptimization_TableCapacityMode.html

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] Calculated throughput-only break-even is u*=hourly capacity-unit price/(3600 × request-unit price). Those US East rates give 28.89% for reads or writes: provisioned is cheaper above it and on-demand below it, excluding discounts, free allowances and other charges. Usage.ai independently presents this calculation; Kerbel applies the same method to Paris prices. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30) — https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/, https://mathieukerbel.com/blog/aws-dynamodb
- [statement] Worked derivation: 100 WCUs for 730 hours cost $47.45 and can serve 262.8 million 1-KB standard writes. On-demand costs $164.25 at full utilization, $16.425 at 10%, and $114.975 at 70%. Break-even is $47.45/$164.25=28.89%, before exclusions. Compute read and write bills separately, then sum them. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-05) — https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] AWS's July 7, 2025 guidance recommends on-demand below 30% monthly utilization, says 30–45% can still favor on-demand after operational costs, and says provisioned may suit utilization above 45%. These practical ranges include capacity-management concerns beyond the roughly 29% rate-only equality. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-07) — https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/how-to-evaluate-throughput-utilization-for-amazon-dynamodb-tables-in-provisioned-mode/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] AWS guidance is broader than the rate crossover: its developer guide says on-demand costs less below 35% average utilization, while its July 7, 2025 blog recommends switching below 30% and evaluating TCO at 30–45%. These are published heuristics, not an exact derivation of 28.89%. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CostOptimization_TableCapacityMode.html · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/how-to-evaluate-throughput-utilization-for-amazon-dynamodb-tables-in-provisioned-mode/, https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Reserved provisioned capacity and eligible free-tier capacity change the break-even. Amortize reservation upfront fees over the commitment and include recurring charges and unused commitments. Current AWS pricing also lists Database Savings Plans for both modes and says they cannot stack with reserved capacity for the same workload. Recalculate with effective eligible prices. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30) — https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://mathieukerbel.com/blog/aws-dynamodb, https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] A predictable peak can favor provisioned capacity with a scheduled increase before traffic arrives; unpredictable peaks and long idle periods can favor on-demand. A monthly request total alone cannot establish feasible provisioned capacity, because minimums, headroom and throttling risk affect paid capacity-hours. (high confidence) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CostOptimization_TableCapacityMode.html · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://mathieukerbel.com/blog/aws-dynamodb
- [statement] A nominal 70% auto-scaling target does not ensure 70% realized utilization: minima, scaling delays and headroom can leave paid capacity idle. Model capacity required in each interval and review throttling; a monthly average request count alone cannot establish the cheaper mode. (high confidence) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CostOptimization_TableCapacityMode.html · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] Infracost publishes a policy favoring on-demand for intermittently used non-production tables and flags provisioned Terraform configurations. Its own caveat says continuous high-volume load tests can favor provisioned; environment labels alone do not establish savings. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-03-27) — https://www.infracost.io/resources/finops-policies/dynamodb-consider-using-on-demand-tables · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] For Standard tables in US East (N. Virginia), the cited list rates are $0.625/million WRUs and $0.125/million RRUs on-demand, versus $0.00065/WCU-hour and $0.00013/RCU-hour provisioned. These exclude discounts, free tier and separately billed features. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-05) — https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] Measure actual provisioned utilization over representative traffic, including tables and GSIs. With changing capacity, compare total consumed units against integrated provisioned-unit-seconds, rather than an unweighted average of utilization percentages. AWS recommends at least a month of history and finer CloudWatch periods to expose bursts; a configured 70% target does not prove 70% realized utilization. (high confidence) — https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/how-to-evaluate-throughput-utilization-for-amazon-dynamodb-tables-in-provisioned-mode/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] Kerbel’s original Paris model illustrates why peak timing matters: scheduled provisioned capacity plus a 70% target costs $93.01/month versus $225.03 on-demand, while holding peak capacity all month costs $507.20. This is an illustrative calculation using September 11, 2026 offer prices, not observed customer savings. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-17) — https://mathieukerbel.com/blog/aws-dynamodb · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Normalize requests into units before comparing: reads round in 4-KB increments, writes in 1-KB increments; eventual reads consume half the strong-read units and transactional operations double ordinary units. Account for index consumption and separately billed storage, backups and replication in total cost. (high confidence) — https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even · also: https://www.usage.ai/blogs/aws/reserved-instances/dynamodb/on-demand-vs-provisioned/
- [statement] ScyllaDB's open-source DynamoDB pricing-comparison tool documents a measurement asymmetry: provisioned-table figures represent provisioned capacity, while on-demand figures default to average consumed units per second over 30 days. Its configurable time range helps select representative traffic, but its competitor-comparison output must not be treated as proof of achieved provisioned utilization. (low confidence) — https://github.com/scylladb/dynamodb-pricing-comparison · keywords: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned break-even
